words: All the living and nonliving things in one place that interact with each other.
The place where an organism lives and finds what it needs: food, water, shelter, and space.
An effect or change caused by something, like a new road changing where animals can live.
Something living things need to survive. Clean water, food, shelter, and space are all resources.
Harmful materials, like trash, chemicals, or dirty water, added to the environment in ways that damage it.
The work of protecting and caring for natural resources and living things so they can survive and thrive.

parts.title: Humans Use Ecosystem Resources
parts.html:
Every day, people use things that come from ecosystems: water, wood, soil, food, and land. We need these resources to live, just like other animals do.

When people use resources, they often change the habitat for plants and animals that already live there. Even a small change, like a new path through the woods or a parking lot next to a creek, can change what living things can find.

parts.title: When Human Actions Harm
parts.html:
Some human actions make it harder for living things to survive. Trash and pollution dirty the water. Cutting down forests takes away shelter. Paving land takes away space, and rain runs off the pavement instead of soaking in.

The impact doesn't have to be huge to matter. One pond full of litter can drive away fish, frogs, and the birds that eat them.

parts.title: When Human Actions Help
parts.html:
People can also protect and restore ecosystems. Planting native wildflowers gives bees food. Picking up trash clears harmful things from water and soil. This work is called conservation.

A solution that only looks nice isn't really working. It has to give back food, water, shelter, or space. In the Florida Everglades, people are bringing back fresh water that canals blocked, and wading birds are starting to return to some areas.

compare.testDo: Put the sponge under one tray and the plastic lid under the other: drag them, or tap one, then a tray. Press Pour the rain. Then swap and pour again.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. A sponge and a lid stand in for real ground.

Asponge.text: The sponge soaked up the rain, just like soil, leaves, and roots do. Very little water ran away.

Alid.text: The rain ran right off the lid. But forest ground is soft and full of tiny spaces. Try the sponge here.

Bsponge.text: The sponge soaked it up. But pavement is hard, with no spaces for water. Try the lid here.

Blid.text: The rain ran right off the lid, just like it runs off pavement. It rushed away, carrying bits of trash toward a drain.

mix.q: A town replaces a field of wildflowers with a neat green lawn. It looks nicer. Does it help bees and butterflies?

options.t: Yes. It looks neat and green, so it must help.
options.miss: Looks aren't evidence. Think about resources: does a lawn give bees food?

options.t: No. A lawn gives bees and butterflies almost no food, so it doesn't help them.
options.ok: Yes! A solution only helps if it gives living things food, water, shelter, or space. A lawn looks nice, but it has almost no flowers for bees.

wow.title: The pink birds that need shallow water
wow.alt: A pink roseate spoonbill with a long, flat, spoon-shaped bill feeding in shallow water
wow.caption: A roseate spoonbill feeding · Everglades National Park, Florida (NPS photo)
wow.html:
Roseate spoonbills sweep their spoon-shaped bills side to side through shallow water to catch small fish and shrimp. When canals drained the Everglades, they lost many feeding spots.

Now Florida and the U.S. government are working on one of the biggest wetland restorations ever, sending fresh water south again. Scientists count the birds each year to see if the plan is working.
wow.insetCap: A canal lock built to drain the Everglades, about 1915.

keyIdea: Human actions can harm or help ecosystems by changing the resources organisms need: food, water, shelter, and space. When resources disappear, organisms struggle to survive. When resources are restored, organisms can return and thrive.
